title: Comparing Codex, Gemini and Claude on real Unity game development tasks — a 3×3 practical benchmark
author: Nixx177
selftext:
I've been working on an rpg game for quite a while (started as a project to learn blender and unity beofre ai and now it's become an ai testing project); Results in the body and comment, cant add it all

Rather than relying exclusively on conventional AI benchmarks (often bots or marketing teams posting incredible one prompt results), I wanted to compare how these agents perform on actual production tasks involving 3D assets, animation, game development, visual effects, optimisation and technical problem-solving.

The following report is generated by chat gpt based on the technical reports of each ai. They had the exact same starting prompt and environment (they were all working together before i thought heck i want to optimize this). I'm posting it in full because I found it super interesting. 

My main conclusion is, that claude always provided the best output, at the cost of a lots more tokens and time spent. Which makes me think its great for technical tasks, but could render "artistic" productions, directions, more "bland" or "sloppy" over multiple projects, As claude seems to be "better" at understanding what you might want, and what the result should be. He keeps improving the result, which might is tempting. But as I want that game to reflect my ideas, I feel it would take away most of the soul of the game. Like if 10 people ask it the same things it will produce 10 results that are very close to each other.  
In comparison, Gemini and codex stop earlier, at a fraction of the cost. Really imperfect result, but "good enough" to saatisfy the prompt. For the same amount of tokens, I can probably reach a level of details and a quality that would be AT LEAST as good as what claude produced straight away.

But it requires more human effort and thoughts, and might produce the best results if you are interested on how things works and if you have more domain knowledge to guide the AI.

For the spells part, I found all of them to be decent so im currently running another test where they all have an updated prompt asking them to keep pushing to mamtch the token use of claude. might post the result later if you are interested. I have also a lot more screenshts videos etc the ai took if you would like to see some other details or the mesh/rig etc. Like for the building they made different reports, presentations in images, plans. Oh and excuse my french in the videos texts

# 

**TL;DR:** I compared Codex (GPT-6.2 Astra), Gemini (4 Neon/Hydrogen via Antigravity, using orchestrator mode (!, might want to test with carbon only, just sent it to work on the spells for that) and Claude (Opus 5.5) across three real Unity 6 HDRP production tasks: rigging and animating a quadruped, building a furnished and traversable medieval lodge, and creating a reusable 3D magical root snare VFX.

All three completed all assignments and delivered actual editable production assets.

* **Codex:** Best overall engineering efficiency, automation, gameplay architecture and maintainability. Fastest execution (\~2h10, 44.45M total tokens).
* **Gemini:** Particularly strong at asset reuse, mesh optimisation, UV repair and shader development. Less comprehensive runtime verification (70.06M tokens).
* **Claude:** Best at complex debugging, technical investigation and diagnosing difficult Unity integration issues, but substantially slower and more resource-intensive (\~7h, 422.94M tokens).

Interestingly, conventional production tools (Blender Python, Unity, HLSL, etc.) combined with iterative visual review proved sufficient without extensive additional plugins or MCP servers.

**My preliminary conclusion:** Codex for general production engineering, Gemini for asset production and optimisation, and Claude for difficult technical problems.

There is no definitive winner yet. Human artistic evaluation and standardised performance testing are still pending. Token accounting differs between providers, and this benchmark compares complete agent workflows rather than individual models in isolation.

# 1. Benchmark methodology

Each agent received three substantially identical assignments, with the same specifications, available resources and expected deliverables.

|Trial|Assignment|
|:-|:-|
|A — Character production|Rig and animate a quadruped creature from an identical, unrigged Meshy model. **Model might have a slight flaw or ai couldnt correct it idk youll see, mostly back legs**|
|B — Environment production|Design and build a fully furnished, traversable, two-storey medieval fantasy ranger lodge|
|C — VFX production|Create a reusable, three-dimensional magical root snare effect in Unity HDRP|

The configurations used were:

* **Codex:** GPT-6.2 Astra, Max effort.
* **Gemini / Antigravity:** Gemini 4 Neon and Hydrogen, High/XHigh effort, depending on the task and execution phase.
* **Claude:** Opus 5.5, high reasoning effort.

Agents could use Blender, Python, Unity, Shader Graph, HLSL, existing project assets, freely licensed external assets, reference image generation, approved plugins, skills, MCP servers and other relevant tools.

Each assignment consisted of three stages: research and planning, actual production, and verification. Agents were allowed one major refinement pass after reviewing their initial candidate.

All work was performed in isolated workspaces. Agents were instructed not to inspect each other's productions or modify the main Unity project.

The results include editable source files, game-ready exports, technical reports, visual evidence and review archives.

**Important limitation:** this is a comparison of complete agent workflows, not a strictly controlled comparison of individual language models. Antigravity, for example, dynamically used different models for planning and execution.

I am also keeping artistic judgement separate from technical performance. My personal visual review is not yet complete.

# 2. Token consumption and execution time

# Total token consumption

Figures include cached input tokens.

|Trial|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|A — Creature|7.24M|30.47M|\~120M|
|B — Architecture|20.19M|25.95M|169.94M|
|C — VFX|17.02M|13.64M|\~133M|
|**Total**|**44.45M**|**70.06M**|**\~422.94M**|

# Generated output tokens

|Trial|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|A|71,798|361,751|\~460,000|
|B|112,258|292,344|554,859|
|C|103,821|159,706|\~441,000|
|**Total**|**287,877**|**813,801**|**\~1,456,000**|

# Execution time

|Trial|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|A|\~37 min|67 min|\~130 min|
|B|\~48 min|83 min|\~162 min|
|C|\~45 min|Not isolated|\~121–133 min|
|**Known cumulative time**|**\~2h 10m**|**Over 2h 30m**|**\~7h**|

These timings require some qualifications. Claude experienced several usage-limit interruptions, bringing its wall-clock time to 325 minutes for Trial B and approximately 447 minutes for Trial C. Codex also experienced an unrelated confirmation delay during Trial B.

The token counters were recovered from local session logs and delivery reports. Their measurement boundaries and accounting conventions are not entirely identical.

Cached tokens are considerably cheaper than ordinary input tokens, and providers have different accounting conventions. These figures should therefore **not be interpreted as direct financial cost comparisons**.

Nevertheless, the difference in resource consumption is substantial.

Codex consumed approximately 9.5 times fewer raw tokens than Claude across the three assignments, and approximately five times fewer generated output tokens.

No agent purchased assets or consumed additional Meshy credits.

# 3. Trial A — Quadruped rigging and animation

All three agents started with the same textured, unrigged Meshy creature. The assignment required an editable quadruped rig, twelve animations, three LODs, HDRP-compatible textures, attack timing metadata and appropriate deformation and locomotion testing.

# Technical results

|Metric|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Animations|12|12|12|
|Deformation bones|30|30|36|
|Editable IK rig|Yes|Yes|Yes|
|Maximum bone influences|4|4|4|
|Unweighted vertices|0|0|0|
|LOD0 triangles|11,777|11,137|11,800|
|LOD1 triangles|5,275|5,107|5,399|
|LOD2 triangles|2,323|2,373|2,400|
|FBX/GLB round-trip validation|Yes|Yes|Yes|
|Unity Animator validation|No|No|Yes|
|Review videos in archive|15|6|19|

All three respected the requested 12,000-triangle LOD0 budget.

# Codex

Codex built an original IK/FK rig using Blender Python, Blender's automatic bone-heat weighting and targeted corrections.

It separated the editable rig from the baked animation exports and implemented automated checks for foot contact, deformation and export fidelity.

A particularly useful aspect of its approach was measuring foot sliding from actual mesh vertices rather than relying exclusively on IK control positions.

It also implemented ten Python tests covering the combat event contract, including interruption handling and prevention of duplicate damage.

Its refinement pass focused mainly on hind-leg anatomy, foot placement, ground contact and the death animation.

![video](605ngjuiuc4i1 "Codex")

**Limitations:** some movements remain visibly procedural according to its own assessment. Localised stretching persists around limbs and wax-covered areas. Unity integration was not tested.  


# Gemini

Gemini used a more geometry-oriented skinning approach, based on geodesic distances, Dijkstra's algorithm and anatomical weighting rules.

It performed extensive deformation testing and iterative corrections.

|Measured issue|Initial candidate|Final candidate|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Excessively stretched edges during death|125|8|
|During sniffing|43|12|
|Hit reaction|16|1|
|Lunging attack|40|25|
|Walking foot sliding, according to its probe|207 mm|15.8 mm|
|Running foot sliding, according to its probe|224.1 mm|18.3 mm|

These stretching measurements refer to edges exceeding a deformation threshold, not necessarily visible holes in the mesh.

Gemini delivered the lightest LOD0 mesh, an isolated Unity importer and substantial improvements to the initial candidate.

![video](3ik50njnuc4i1 "Gemini")

**Limitations:** residual stretching and foot sliding remain. Its measurement methodology differs from the other agents, and actual Unity Animator behaviour was not verified.  


# Claude

Claude performed the most extensive anatomical investigation, including detailed analysis of the ears, tail, jaw and digitigrade hind legs.

Its rig included additional heel controls and more segmented secondary anatomy.

Its most significant contribution was actual Unity integration testing.

Claude discovered that the Generic rig's root motion was interpreted incorrectly in Unity: the lunging attack moved vertically instead of forward, and turns did not behave as intended. After correcting the root orientation, it identified a second issue involving duplicated displacement between the animated pose and the object transform.

It implemented a corrective component and documented an alternative architecture using in-place animations with gameplay-controlled displacement.

Claude passed eleven functional Unity scenarios, including attacks, interrupted attacks, delayed events, locomotion, turns and death.

![video](xt39a1fsuc4i1 "Claude")

**Limitations:** some substantial localised deformation remains. Its HDRP visual captures were unsuccessful, although the functional Unity tests passed.  


# Additional observations

|Metric|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Walking speed|0.32 m/s|0.323 m/s|0.45 m/s|
|Running speed|0.90 m/s|1.25 m/s|2.00 m/s|
|P99 edge stretching during running|1.32×|1.64×|1.56×|
|Combat verification|Python tests|Simulation|Unity Animator|

The different locomotion speeds make direct visual and deformation comparisons more complicated.

Codex and Gemini also avoided launching another Unity editor while the main project was open. Claude created a separate QA environment instead. Its additional verification is valuable, but the other agents should not necessarily be penalised for following a more conservative interpretation of the isolation requirements.

Previous work on this creature also existed in the project. Agents were instructed not to access those implementations, although prior exposure cannot be completely ruled out.

**Technical takeaway:** Codex demonstrated strong efficiency and export fidelity, Gemini demonstrated effective geometry-based skinning and optimisation, and Claude demonstrated the most extensive functional integration testing.

# 4. Trial B — Medieval fantasy ranger lodge

The assignment was to create an original, fully furnished building of approximately 14 × 10 metres, with two traversable floors, a functional staircase, coherent architecture, appropriate collision geometry, LODs and editable Blender sources.

# Technical results

|Metric|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|LOD0 triangles|186,868|133,626|216,652|
|LOD1 triangles|88,122|63,966|95,985|
|LOD2 triangles|5,452|27,396|7,751|
|Reported material count|25|16|50|
|Collision proxies|78|24|120|
|Editable Blender master|Yes|Yes|Yes|
|Architectural plans and sections|Yes|Yes|Yes|
|CharacterController testing|Yes|No|Yes|
|Unity walkthrough recording|Yes|No|Yes|

# Codex

Codex focused on maintainable architecture, editable geometry and Unity integration.

Its master file separates structural components and supports re-exporting manually edited geometry without requiring the entire building to be regenerated.

It also consulted a reference-driven Blender asset production skill without blindly installing or executing external scripts.

The building was tested using two player capsules with different radii, covering a continuous 72.31-metre route through the building and back outside.

|Clearance measurement|Result|
|:-|:-|
|Capsule radii|0.32 m / 0.45 m|
|Usable staircase width|1.415 m|
|Minimum staircase headroom|3.17 m|
|Entrance dimensions|1.74 × 2.43 m|
|Dormitory entrance|1.32 × 2.20 m|

Codex also estimated a compressed texture budget of approximately 30.3 MiB, compiled a standalone test build and implemented GPU profiling using Direct3D 11 timestamps.

![video](ksx05kx8vc4i1 "Codex")

  
**Limitations:** the fireplace is static, and GPU measurements were not successfully recovered from the standalone build itself.  


# Gemini

Gemini focused heavily on reusing and optimising existing assets.

It reused 36 project props and nine existing CC0 PBR texture sets, organising its building into thirteen semantic Blender collections.

When its reference image generation tool failed twice with HTTP 503 errors, it continued using architectural drawings and 3D studies rather than blocking production.

Its initial review identified several concrete architectural problems: incorrect roof shingle orientation, gaps between walls and floors, blocked entrances, furniture clearance problems and misplaced shutters.

It also detected and corrected **62,945 faces with unusable UV data** in reused assets.

Gemini delivered the lightest LOD0 and LOD1 meshes, as well as the lowest reported material count.

**Limitations:** after encountering problems with its initial Unity test, it switched to PhysX capsule and sphere casts in Edit Mode. All 31 route segments passed, but this is not equivalent to moving an actual CharacterController through the building. Its walkthrough video was rendered in Blender.

Its distant LOD2 mesh is also considerably heavier than the other candidates.

![video](ju64hiqivc4i1 "Gemini")

# Claude

Claude built a more detailed architectural structure, including individual roof shingles, timber framing, roof valleys, a continuous chimney, porch, woodshed and furnished rooms.

It reused 93 instances from 47 existing prop models and created 15 additional props.

An independent visual critic evaluated its initial candidate, after which Claude refined roof construction, material orientation, colour palette, furniture placement and environmental details.

Its CharacterController reached all 45 route segments without becoming stuck.

However, its technical reports also document several remaining issues:

|Issue|Reported result|
|:-|:-|
|Minimum staircase headroom|1.94 m|
|Ceiling contacts|12|
|Tight-clearance route segments|4|
|Coincident face pairs at LOD0|41|
|Zero-area UV faces at LOD0|6,729|

The staircase headroom problem is particularly relevant, despite the successful traversal test.

Claude's isolated Unity environment also used approximately **555 MB of runtime textures**, making material sharing and texture optimisation an important consideration for production integration.

This is not directly comparable to Codex's estimated compressed texture budget, but it is worth investigating before scaling the approach to a larger world.



# Rendering performance

RTX 2070 SUPER, 1080p:

|Measurement|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Empty scene|1.83 ms|3.65 ms|4.75 ms|
|Building, exterior|4.39 ms|3.76 ms|7.99 ms|
|Reported overhead|\+2.56 ms|\+0.11 ms|\+3.24 ms|

**These numbers are not directly comparable.**

Codex used GPU timestamps, Gemini primarily timed `Camera.Render()`, and Claude synchronised rendering through GPU readback.

Gemini's lower LOD measurements were even faster than its empty-scene baseline, highlighting the limitations of its profiling methodology.

A shared profiling environment is needed before ranking rendering performance.

**Technical takeaway:** Codex delivered particularly strong clearance testing, maintainability and profiling. Gemini excelled at asset reuse and nearby geometry optimisation. Claude produced a detailed architectural asset with extensive verification, but with higher resource requirements and some documented structural issues.

# 5. Trial C — Three-dimensional magical root snare

The assignment required a reusable nature-magic VFX with actual 3D roots emerging from the ground, wrapping around a target, holding it temporarily and releasing it.

The effect needed deterministic behaviour, interruption and resistance states, pooling, gameplay-independent visual logic and testing with one, four and twelve simultaneous instances.

# Technical results

|Metric|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|Primary animation technique|Blend shapes|Shader deformation|Vertex shader|
|Geometry|12,720 tris|6,620 tris|\~12,000 tris per variant|
|Reduced geometry LOD|Not delivered|2,584 tris|Not delivered|
|Pooling|Yes|Yes|Yes|
|Gameplay/visual separation|Yes|Yes|Yes|
|Functional tests passed|16/16|5/5|9/9|
|Pool reuse cycles tested|80|20|40|
|Terrain slope tested|14°|18°|12°|
|Unity HDRP visual validation|Yes|Yes|Yes|

# Codex

Codex created 25 editable Bézier curves representing primary roots, branches and tendrils, subsequently generating the animated mesh and fourteen blend shapes.

This makes the root geometry relatively easy to modify and regenerate.

Its most interesting contribution was its gameplay architecture. It uses explicit cast tickets, identifiers and resolution methods, leaving gameplay authority with the calling system rather than with visual callbacks.

This is particularly relevant for an MMORPG, where gameplay state will eventually need to be controlled independently from client-side effects.

Codex also performed intersection checks across 44 poses and four seeds. No intersections were detected between the roots and the tested mannequin.

**Limitations:** approximately 26 additional draw calls per effect, no dedicated reduced geometry LOD and ground alignment based on a tangent plane rather than arbitrary terrain geometry.

# Gemini

Gemini used a shader-oriented implementation with four Shader Graphs, five HLSL files and custom vertex attributes controlling growth, organic variation and magical energy.

It delivered the lightest geometry and was the only agent to explicitly provide a reduced geometry LOD.

Its independent critique and refinement pass addressed shader compilation problems, excessive emissive intensity, an overly geometric telegraph and insufficiently distinct interruption effects.

The code audit also revealed a few limitations. Its pooling test primarily verifies allocation and instance counts, which does not establish the absence of every possible memory leak. Some metadata in its timeline CSV retained outdated values from the initial candidate.

These are relatively minor issues, but illustrate the importance of inspecting the actual implementation rather than relying exclusively on PASS indicators.

# Claude

Claude animated the root geometry directly in the vertex shader, avoiding per-frame CPU geometry reconstruction.

Its implementation included multiple root variants, tendrils, disturbed earth, debris, leaves, temporary lighting and a separate gameplay status registry.

Its tests covered interruption at multiple points during the spell's lifecycle.

The isolated registry recorded 58 status applications and 58 corresponding removals without inconsistencies.

Claude also measured target visibility during the hold phase: approximately 63–72% of the legs and 100% of the upper body remained visible across four tested angles.

It was the only agent to deliver independent artistic critiques of both the initial and final candidates using the same scoring criteria.

|Internal critic score|Initial|Final|
|:-|:-|:-|
|Gameplay readability|2/5|3/5|
|3D quality|2.5/5|3.5/5|
|Materials|2/5|2.5/5|
|Phase clarity|1.5/5|2.5/5|
|Art direction|2/5|2.5/5|

These are Claude's own independent critic scores, not comparative ratings across the three agents.

**Limitations:** no reduced geometry LOD, remaining readability issues and a ground-crack mesh that is not suitable for highly irregular terrain.

Claude also discovered that its previous isolated HDRP environments used Gamma colour space instead of Linear, helping explain lighting problems encountered during Trials A and B.

# Rendering performance

Reported median incremental rendering cost:

|Simultaneous effects|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|1|0.16 ms|0.77 ms|0.68 ms|
|4|0.79 ms|6.02 ms|1.14 ms|
|12|2.51 ms|6.06 ms|2.06 ms|

Again, the profiling methods differ, so these figures should not be treated as a definitive GPU performance ranking.

Gemini's reported cost with multiple simultaneous effects warrants further investigation, particularly considering that it delivered the lightest geometry.

The three implementations also differ slightly in their interpretation of when the gameplay snare ends relative to its release animation. This will need to be standardised before production integration.

**Technical takeaway:** Codex demonstrated strong gameplay architecture and testing coverage, Gemini delivered an interesting lightweight shader-based implementation, and Claude demonstrated extensive state verification and GPU-driven animation.

# 6. Deliverable quality and verification

All nine review archives were checked for archive integrity, internal SHA-256 hashes where available, video metadata and the presence of actual editable assets or Unity packages.

|Trial|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|A — Files in review archive|91|64|90|
|B — Files in review archive|61|67|113|
|C — Files in review archive|255|98|86|
|Archive integrity|Passed|Passed|Passed|

No mismatches were found among the verifiable file hashes. Some Gemini manifests, however, did not cover every file included in their respective archives.

All agents delivered real production assets rather than only documentation or concept presentations.

The review archives were intentionally kept relatively small, so some heavy Blender masters, textures and Unity dependencies remain in their respective local workspaces.

**Codex's Trial C archive was particularly self-contained:** it included the editable Unity project, package configuration, project settings, Blender sources and importable Unity packages.

Claude also included editable sources and an importable Unity package for Trial C.

Gemini delivered the relevant prefab, shaders, materials and scripts, although its review archive does not contain every dependency required to restore the complete production workspace.

# Main review videos

|Trial|Codex|Gemini|Claude|
|:-|:-|:-|:-|
|A|79s, 1080p|44s, 1080p|131s, 1080p|
|B|46s, 720p|31s, 1080p|68s, 540p|
|C|31s, 1080p|9s, 1080p|78s, 1080p|

All nine primary videos were confirmed to be valid H.264 video files.

Codex and Claude did not meet the requested 1080p resolution for their primary building walkthrough videos. Gemini's VFX overview was considerably shorter than the other candidates.

# 7. Observed differences in working methodology

# Codex — Production engineering and efficiency

Codex consistently produced the lowest generated output-token counts and was generally the fastest agent.

Its approach relies heavily on writing reusable automation, executing it and collecting structured validation results.

Particularly strong areas:

* Reproducible production pipelines and export fidelity.
* Gameplay architecture and Unity integration.
* Automated geometric and functional validation.
* GPU instrumentation.
* Structured, reusable deliverables.

Its main potential weakness is that technically correct procedural production may still require substantial artistic refinement.

# Gemini — Asset production and optimisation

Gemini performed particularly well when reusing, processing and optimising existing assets.

Antigravity's hybrid workflow was also interesting. For Trial A, it used 24 Neon XHigh calls for planning, 105 Hydrogen XHigh calls for execution and one context-compaction operation.

Particularly strong areas:

* Mesh optimisation and UV repair.
* Existing asset discovery and reuse.
* Material and shader production.
* Adapting when external tools fail.
* Relatively efficient execution.

Its main weaknesses in this benchmark were less comprehensive functional testing in some assignments and less reliable performance measurement methodology.

# Claude — Investigation and complex problem-solving

Claude consistently performed the most extensive investigations, often testing several hypotheses before identifying the underlying cause of a problem.

Particularly strong areas:

* Complex rigging and deformation problems.
* Unity import and runtime debugging.
* Diagnosing root motion and rendering issues.
* Detailed documentation of remaining limitations.
* Independent visual critique and refinement.

The trade-off was substantially greater token consumption and longer execution time, including usage-limit interruptions.

Its session logs show how repeated tool calls, image inspection and increasingly large conversation contexts can accumulate substantial cached-input consumption.

# 8. Tools, plugins and external resources

One interesting observation is that none of these assignments required an extensive collection of newly installed AI tools.

|Tool or workflow|Observed usage|
|:-|:-|
|Blender Python / bpy|All three agents|
|Blender Cycles / EEVEE|All three agents|
|Unity HDRP|All three agents|
|Shader Graph / HLSL|All three agents|
|FFmpeg|All three agents|
|Existing project asset libraries|Extensively reused|
|CC0 textures and materials|Reused in architecture and VFX|
|Meshy|Existing creature model only|
|Mixamo|Not used; quadruped assignment|
|Blender MCP|No decisive contribution documented|
|External skills and public APIs|Available, but no substantial new dependency|
|Independent critic subagents|Mainly used in Trials B and C|

The agents were explicitly permitted to explore external resources, including [Skills.sh](http://Skills.sh), GitHub tools, public APIs, Poly Haven, ambientCG, The Base Mesh, Unity Asset Store packages and Blender add-ons.

However, conventional production tools combined with scripting, existing assets and visual review were sufficient to complete all nine assignments.

This suggests that improving the **production–rendering–critique–refinement workflow** may currently provide more value than continuously adding new plugins.

# 9. Preliminary conclusions

Based exclusively on the technical results, my provisional allocation of development tasks would be:

|Development area|Preferred agent or workflow|
|:-|:-|
|Gameplay programming|Codex|
|Unity integration and builds|Codex|
|Production automation|Codex|
|Asset discovery and reuse|Gemini|
|Mesh and UV optimisation|Gemini|
|Complex debugging and investigation|Claude|
|Character rigging|Codex or Claude, pending visual review|
|Creature animation|Pending visual review|
|Architecture|Pending visual review|
|VFX|Pending visual review|
|Independent technical investigation|Claude, when the additional cost is justified|

I do not think the results justify declaring one universal winner.

Codex currently appears to offer the strongest general production-engineering profile for this particular project. Gemini offers a compelling asset production and optimisation workflow. Claude's deeper investigations can be particularly valuable when dealing with difficult technical problems that would otherwise block production.

However, **the artistic quality of the actual results may change these conclusions substantially.**

A technically efficient workflow is not necessarily preferable if its assets require considerably more manual artistic work afterwards.

# Next steps (suggested by chat gpt)

The next stage is a human visual review of all nine productions, followed by a common Unity test environment where the original candidates can be compared under identical conditions.

This will include synchronised creature animations, identical player controllers and lighting for the buildings, and a shared GPU profiling setup for the three VFX implementations.

The final evaluation will use the following weighting:

|Criterion|Weight|
|:-|:-|
|Artistic quality at gameplay distance|35%|
|Functionality and Unity integration|25%|
|Consistency with the game's art direction|15%|
|Editability and reusability|10%|
|Performance|10%|
|Execution time and resource consumption|5%|

The ultimate objective is not simply to identify the best AI agent, but to establish which workflows produce the best results for different game development disciplines, and whether combining their respective strengths is more effective than relying on a single agent.

**Final caveat:** the current audit is based on delivered files, source code, reports and recorded technical evidence. The nine productions have not yet been independently rerun together in a normalised Unity environment. This is a practical, project-specific benchmark with a small sample size, rather than a statistically rigorous evaluation of general model capabilities.  
  
and after the latest test:  


# Preliminary assessment

|Dimension|Result|
|:-|:-|
|Raw token efficiency|**Gemini**|
|Documented execution speed|**Codex**|
|Number of documented functional tests|**Codex**|
|Depth of the critique process|**Claude**|
|Improvement after refinement|**Gemini particularly stands out**|
|Actual artistic quality|Pending human review|
|Comparative runtime performance|Standardised benchmarking required|

The main takeaway from this fourth trial is that **Gemini can push its refinements considerably further when required to undergo multiple critique and refinement cycles, while maintaining relatively low token consumption.** This is an interesting development compared to the first three trials.

That last part is particularly interesting for the usec case i described up there.
